newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan to tackle bad debts of state banks.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan to tackle bad debts of state banks.

text.p: Pakistan's privatisation chief said on Sunday a loan recovery trust devised by the departing caretaker government would be a crucial tool in preparing the ailing state-owned banking sector for privatisation.

President Farooq Leghari issued a decree on Friday establishing the Resolution Trust Corporation of Pakistan (RTCP) to assume bad debts worth an estimated 130 billion rupees ($3.23 billion) at state-run banks and financial institutions.

"The RTCP should come into operation very quickly and then in the financial sector we should be able to go ahead with reforms," Salman Shah, chairman of the Privatisation Commission, told Reuters. "We should be able to start clearing the bad loans, which is very essential for privatisation."

"The RTCP will be dedicated to the acquisition, holding, restructuring and disposition of the non-performing assets of financial institutions," said Haroon Sharif, a private banker involved in planning the RTCP's creation.

"The RTCP will buy bad debts from banks and issue bonds saying the government will pay back the amount in seven years," he said. "In the process, an interest (rate) of 10 to 12 percent may be offered on the bond."
Sharif said that about 30 billion rupees of the total 130 billion rupees of non-performing loans represented interest and penalties that might simply be written off.
"Realistically, we may be able to recover about 70 to 80 billion rupees in the seven-year time period," Sharif said.

By isolating the non-performing assets at the RTCP, the government will be able to deal more effectively with the overall reform and privatisation of state-run financial institutions, a goal agreed with the World Bank, he said.

"The government-owned banking sector cannot collect bad debts because of political influence. But once the RTCP takes away the bad debts, the banks' books become clean and attractive for privatisation," he said.
Sharif said a large number of loan defaulters in Pakistan were influential people who would resist repaying their debts.
"The intentional defaulter mostly relies on political influence and may be responsible for 60 percent of the defaults," he added.
He warned that the RTCP would fail unless the next government kept it free of political interference.
The caretaker government of Prime Minister Meraj Khalid is due to hand over power to the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) on Monday after the PML's landslide victory in February 3 polls.
Sharif said the RTCP would free up man-hours now spent by state banks on trying to collect their bad debts.
The ordinance gives the RTCP special recovery powers and provides for special tribunals to be set up for legal cases.
Shah said the RTCP's effectiveness depended on the attitude of the incoming government led by Nawaz Sharif.
"Without the full support of the government nobody can succeed," he said. ($1 = 40 rupees)
